q: Fluid is a substance that offers no permanent resistance to deforming forces.
e: True. Fluid is a substance that offers no permanent resistance to deforming forces. A fluid yields steadily under shear; it does not keep a fixed shape.

q: Fluid statics concentrates on fluids in motion, while fluid dynamics concerns with the fluids at rest.
e: False. Fluid statics studies fluids at rest. The error is the part about Fluid statics concentrates fluids motion dynamics.

q: Motion of fluids can be classified by two types, laminar flow and turbulent flow.
e: True. Motion of fluids can be classified by two types, laminar flow and turbulent flow. Laminar flow moves in smooth layers with no mixing between neighbouring sheets.

q: If fluid particles are moving steady in smooth paths in layers, with each layer moving smoothly past the adjacent layers with no mixing, such a flow is called turbulent flow.
e: False. Smooth layered motion with no mixing is laminar flow, not turbulent flow. The error is the part about fluid particles moving steady smooth paths.

q: In this steady laminar flow, streamlines do not cross each other.
e: True. In this steady laminar flow, streamlines do not cross each other. A streamline is the path a fluid particle follows. In steady laminar flow, streamlines do not cross.

q: Every fluid particle arriving at a given point has a different velocity in steady laminar flow.
e: False. In steady laminar flow every particle arriving at a given point has the same velocity. The error is the part about Every fluid particle arriving given point.

q: If the flow or path of the fluid particles are irregular, their direction is always changing or whirling, this fluid movement is called turbulent flow.
e: True. If the flow or path of the fluid particles are irregular, their direction is always changing or whirling, this fluid movement is called turbulent flow. Turbulent flow is irregular and whirling, so speed and direction at a point keep changing.

q: In turbulent flow the speed of the fluid at a point is continuously undergoing changes in both magnitude and direction.
e: True. In turbulent flow the speed of the fluid at a point is continuously undergoing changes in both magnitude and direction. Turbulent flow is irregular and whirling, so speed and direction at a point keep changing.

q: The volume of a gas depends on pressure and temperature obeying Boyle's law and Charles' law.
e: True. The volume of a gas depends on pressure and temperature obeying Boyle's law and Charles' law. Gas volume depends on p and T through Boyle and Charles.

q: The volume of a liquid depends heavily on pressure if the temperature is constant.
e: False. A liquid's volume is almost independent of pressure at fixed temperature; liquids are nearly incompressible. The error is the part about volume liquid depends heavily pressure temperature.

q: Ideal laminar fluid flow considers the fluid is compressible.
e: False. Ideal laminar Bernoulli flow treats the fluid as incompressible. The error is the part about Ideal laminar fluid flow considers compressible.

q: Ideal laminar fluid flow considers the flow has no friction or friction is neglected.
e: True. Ideal laminar fluid flow considers the flow has no friction or friction is neglected. Laminar flow moves in smooth layers with no mixing between neighbouring sheets.

q: Internal friction in fluids is called viscosity.
e: True. Internal friction in fluids is called viscosity. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Ideal laminar fluid flow considers high viscosity.
e: False. Ideal Bernoulli flow is non-viscous, so internal friction is neglected. The error is the part about Ideal laminar fluid flow considers high.

q: Ideal laminar fluid flow considers the fluid flow is laminar (steady) and turbulent flow is not taken into account.
e: True. Ideal laminar fluid flow considers the fluid flow is laminar (steady) and turbulent flow is not taken into account. Laminar flow moves in smooth layers with no mixing between neighbouring sheets.

q: Sea breeze is a laminar flow and storm is a turbulent flow.
e: True. Sea breeze is a laminar flow and storm is a turbulent flow. Laminar flow moves in smooth layers with no mixing between neighbouring sheets.

q: Sea breeze is a turbulent flow and storm is a laminar flow.
e: False. A sea breeze is typically smoother laminar-like flow; a storm is turbulent. The error is the part about Sea breeze turbulent flow storm laminar.

q: Consider an ideal fluid there must be laminar flow and no viscosity.
e: True. Consider an ideal fluid there must be laminar flow and no viscosity. Laminar flow moves in smooth layers with no mixing between neighbouring sheets.

q: The density of an ideal fluid is constantly changing.
e: False. An ideal fluid is incompressible, so its density stays constant. The error is the part about density ideal fluid constantly changing.

q: In a pipe, all the liquid that flow through section 1 flow through section 2.
e: True. In a pipe, all the liquid that flow through section 1 flow through section 2. Incompressible continuity: what enters one cross-section leaves the other.

q: The mass flowing in section 1 must be greater than the mass flowing in section 2.
e: False. Continuity keeps mass flow the same through every section of a single pipe. The error is the part about mass flowing section greater.

q: The equation $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ states that the liquid entering one end of the pipe leaves from the other end with a constant volume flow rate.
e: True. The equation A₁ v₁ = A₂ v₂ states that the liquid entering one end of the pipe leaves from the other end with a constant volume flow rate. A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ keeps volume flow rate Av constant along the pipe.

q: The larger the area of the pipe, the slower is the speed.
e: True. The larger the area of the pipe, the slower is the speed. Continuity: Av is constant, so a wide section runs slowly.

q: The smaller the area, the slower is the speed.
e: False. Continuity says smaller area means larger speed, A v = constant. The error is the part about smaller area slower speed.

q: The speed of water spraying from a hose increases by making the hose area smaller.
e: True. The speed of water spraying from a hose increases by making the hose area smaller. A smaller nozzle area raises v so that Av stays the same.

q: The speed of water spraying from a hose decreases by making the hose area smaller.
e: False. Narrowing the nozzle raises the exit speed, it does not lower it. The error is the part about speed water spraying hose decreases making.

q: Bernoulli's equation relates the pressure, flow speed, and height for the steady (laminar) flow of an ideal incompressible fluid.
e: True. Bernoulli's equation relates the pressure, flow speed, and height for the steady (laminar) flow of an ideal incompressible fluid. Laminar flow moves in smooth layers with no mixing between neighbouring sheets.

q: The internal friction of the fluid flow is very high in Bernoulli's equation.
e: False. Bernoulli's equation assumes non-viscous flow, so internal friction is taken as zero. The error is the part about internal friction fluid flow high Bernoulli.

q: Bernoulli's equation can be derived using the work-energy principle to a fluid flowing in a tube.
e: True. Bernoulli's equation can be derived using the work-energy principle to a fluid flowing in a tube. Pressure work on a fluid slug equals the change of its mechanical energy.

q: According to work-energy principle, the work done on this section of fluid must equal the change in total mechanical energy.
e: True. According to work-energy principle, the work done on this section of fluid must equal the change in total mechanical energy. Pressure work on a fluid slug equals the change of its mechanical energy.

q: Total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and thermal energy.
e: False. Mechanical energy here is kinetic plus gravitational potential, not thermal energy. The error is the part about Total mechanical energy sum kinetic thermal.

q: Since the fluid is incompressible, $A_1 \Delta x_1 = A_2 \Delta x_2 = \Delta V$.
e: True. Since the fluid is incompressible, A₁ Δ x₁ = A₂ Δ x₂ = Δ V. Equal volumes A Δx pass both sections because the liquid cannot change density.

q: The work done on the fluid in this case is due to the viscosity of the fluid.
e: False. In the Bernoulli derivation the work is pressure work pΔV, with viscosity neglected. The error is the part about work done fluid case due viscosity.

q: The mass of the fluid between a and b is $\rho \Delta V$.
e: True. The mass of the fluid between a and b is ρ Δ V. That mass is density times the volume slug, m = ρ ΔV.

q: The change in kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2} \rho \Delta V (v_2^2 - v_1^2)$.
e: True. The change in kinetic energy is (1)/(2) ρ Δ V (v₂² - v₁²). ΔK = ½ ρ ΔV (v₂² − v₁²) for that incompressible slug.

q: The change in potential energy is $\rho \Delta V g (h_2 - h_1)$.
e: True. The change in potential energy is ρ Δ V g (h₂ - h₁). ΔU = ρ ΔV g (h₂ − h₁) as the slug changes height.

q: Bernoulli's theorem states that the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume of an incompressible, non-viscous fluid in a streamlined laminar flow remains constant.
e: True. Bernoulli's theorem states that the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume of an incompressible, non-viscous fluid in a streamlined. A streamline is the path a fluid particle follows. In steady laminar flow, streamlines do not cross.

q: Bernoulli's theorem states that the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit mass remains constant.
e: False. Bernoulli's textbook form is per unit volume: p + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. The error is the part about Bernoulli theorem states sum pressure energy.

q: The equation is $p + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}$.
e: True. The equation is p + (1)/(2) ρ v² + ρ g h = constant. Keep the exact quantity, direction or number named in the statement.

q: The air flow moving above the top curved surface of the wing has a longer distance to travel and needs to go faster to have the same transit time as the air travelling along the lower flat surface.
e: True. The air flow moving above the top curved surface of the wing has a longer distance to travel and needs to go faster to have the same transit time as the air travelling. Faster air over the longer top path lowers pressure there and lift appears.

q: The velocity of air flow is low along the top surface and high along the bottom surface of an aeroplane wing.
e: False. Air is faster over the longer top of the wing and slower under the bottom, so pressure is lower above. The error is the part about velocity air flow low along top.

q: This causes a low pressure above the wing and a high pressure below the wing which provides a lift on the wing.
e: True. This causes a low pressure above the wing and a high pressure below the wing which provides a lift on the wing. The pressure difference across the wing is the lift.

q: When the piston of the insect sprayer is pressed, the fast moving air causes a low pressure at the tip of the nozzle.
e: True. When the piston of the insect sprayer is pressed, the fast moving air causes a low pressure at the tip of the nozzle. Bernoulli: high speed, low pressure, so the sprayer sucks liquid up the stem.

q: When the piston of the insect sprayer is pressed, the fast moving air causes a high pressure at the tip of the nozzle.
e: False. Fast air at the sprayer nozzle is low pressure, and that drop draws liquid up the stem. The error is the part about piston insect sprayer pressed fast moving.

q: The liquid inside the container of an insect sprayer is at a higher pressure, and therefore rushes up through the stem and out the nozzle.
e: True. The liquid inside the container of an insect sprayer is at a higher pressure, and therefore rushes up through the stem and out the nozzle. The still liquid sits at higher pressure than the fast nozzle air, so it rushes out.

q: The Magnus effect is a particular manifestation of Bernoulli's theorem that is commonly associated with a spinning object moving through a fluid.
e: True. The Magnus effect is a particular manifestation of Bernoulli's theorem that is commonly associated with a spinning object moving through a fluid. Bernoulli's equation keeps p + ½ρv² + ρgh constant along a streamline for incompressible, non-viscous laminar flow.

q: The Magnus effect is commonly associated with a stationary object moving through a vacuum.
e: False. The Magnus effect needs a spinning object moving through a fluid, not a stationary object in vacuum. The error is the part about Magnus effect commonly associated stationary object.

q: In the case of a ball spinning through the air, the turning ball drags some of the air around with it.
e: True. In the case of a ball spinning through the air, the turning ball drags some of the air around with it. That dragged air plus the oncoming stream is the Magnus effect.

q: During cyclones, moving air gains speed above the roof of a house causing the reduced pressure on the roof.
e: True. During cyclones, moving air gains speed above the roof of a house causing the reduced pressure on the roof. Fast cyclone air above the roof drops the outside pressure.

q: During cyclones, moving air gains speed above the roof of a house causing the increased pressure on the roof.
e: False. Faster air above the roof lowers pressure, it does not increase it. The error is the part about cyclones moving air gains speed above.

q: Therefore the pressure inside the house is greater, which can raise the roof.
e: True. Therefore the pressure inside the house is greater, which can raise the roof. Higher indoor pressure than over the roof can lift the roof.

q: Therefore the pressure inside the house is lower, which can raise the roof.
e: False. The inside pressure is then higher than the roof-top pressure, and that difference can lift the roof. The error is the part about Therefore pressure inside house lower raise.

q: Most of the fluids are not ideal ones and offer some resistance to motion.
e: True. Most of the fluids are not ideal ones and offer some resistance to motion. Real fluids have viscosity, so they resist relative motion of layers.

q: The resistance to fluid motion (or) internal resistance of fluid is called surface tension.
e: False. Internal resistance to flow is viscosity, not surface tension. The error is the part about resistance fluid motion internal surface tension.

q: Viscosity arises when there is relative motion between layers of the fluid.
e: True. Viscosity arises when there is relative motion between layers of the fluid. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Viscosity arises when the fluid is completely at rest.
e: False. Viscosity appears when layers move relative to each other, not when the fluid is fully at rest. The error is the part about Viscosity arises fluid completely rest.

q: Viscosity measures resistance to flow arising due to the internal friction between the fluid layers as they slip past one another when fluid flows.
e: True. Viscosity measures resistance to flow arising due to the internal friction between the fluid layers as they slip past one another when fluid flows. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Viscosity can also be thought of as a measure of a fluid's thickness (stickiness) or its resistance to objects passing through it.
e: True. Viscosity can also be thought of as a measure of a fluid's thickness (stickiness) or its resistance to objects passing through it. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: A fluid with large viscosity resists motion because its strong intermolecular forces give it a lot of internal friction.
e: True. A fluid with large viscosity resists motion because its strong intermolecular forces give it a lot of internal friction. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: A fluid with large viscosity flows easily because its molecular make up results in very little friction when it is in motion.
e: False. Large viscosity means more internal friction, so the fluid does not flow easily. The error is the part about fluid large viscosity flows easily molecular.

q: A fluid with low viscosity flows easily because its molecular make up results in very little friction when it is in motion.
e: True. A fluid with low viscosity flows easily because its molecular make up results in very little friction when it is in motion. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Gases also exhibit viscosity, but it is harder to notice in ordinary circumstances.
e: True. Gases also exhibit viscosity, but it is harder to notice in ordinary circumstances. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: The viscosity of liquids increases rapidly with an increase in temperature.
e: False. Liquid viscosity falls as temperature rises, so heated liquids flow more easily. The error is the part about viscosity liquids increases rapidly increase temperature.

q: The viscosity of liquids decreases rapidly with an increase in temperature.
e: True. The viscosity of liquids decreases rapidly with an increase in temperature. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: The viscosity of gases decreases with an increase in temperature.
e: False. Gas viscosity rises with temperature, so hot gases flow less easily. The error is the part about viscosity gases decreases increase temperature.

q: The viscosity of gases increases with an increase in temperature.
e: True. The viscosity of gases increases with an increase in temperature. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Thus, upon heating, liquids flow more easily, whereas gases flow more slowly.
e: True. Thus, upon heating, liquids flow more easily, whereas gases flow more slowly. Heating cuts liquid viscosity and raises gas viscosity.

q: Thus, upon heating, liquids flow more slowly, whereas gases flow more easily.
e: False. Heating makes liquids run more easily and gases a little more sluggish. The error is the part about Thus upon heating liquids flow slowly.

q: Viscosity does not change as the amount of matter changes, therefore it is an intensive property.
e: True. Viscosity does not change as the amount of matter changes, therefore it is an intensive property. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Viscosity changes as the amount of matter changes, therefore it is an extensive property.
e: False. Viscosity does not depend on the amount of sample, so it is intensive, not extensive. The error is the part about Viscosity changes amount matter therefore extensive.

q: The SI unit of viscosity is pascal second ($Pa \cdot s$) which is equivalent to newton second per metre squared ($N \cdot s \cdot m^{-2}$).
e: True. The SI unit of viscosity is pascal second (Pa · s) which is equivalent to newton second per metre squared (N · s · m⁻²). Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: The SI unit of viscosity is pascal second ($Pa \cdot s$) which is equivalent to newton per metre squared ($N \cdot m^{-2}$).
e: False. Pa·s is N·s/m², not N/m². N/m² is pressure, pascal, without the second.

q: Dynamic viscosity is to measure fluid's resistance to flow when an external force is applied.
e: True. Dynamic viscosity is to measure fluid's resistance to flow when an external force is applied. Dynamic viscosity measures resistance to flow when an external shear is applied.

q: Kinematic viscosity is to measure the resistive flow of a fluid under the weight of gravity.
e: True. Kinematic viscosity is to measure the resistive flow of a fluid under the weight of gravity. Kinematic viscosity is the fluid's resistance to flow under its own weight, dynamic viscosity divided by density.

q: Kinematic viscosity is less useful than dynamic viscosity (absolute viscosity).
e: False. Kinematic viscosity ν = η/ρ is often the handy quantity in free-flow problems. The error is the part about Kinematic viscosity useful dynamic absolute.

q: Newton's law of viscosity states that the shear stress between the two adjacent layers of fluid is directly proportional to the negative value of the velocity gradient between the same two adjacent fluid layers.
e: True. Newton's law of viscosity states that the shear stress between the two adjacent layers of fluid is directly proportional to the negative value of the velocity gradient. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Newton's law of viscosity states that the shear stress is directly proportional to the positive value of the velocity gradient.
e: False. Newton's viscosity law uses the negative velocity gradient between layers. The error is the part about Newton law viscosity states shear stress.

q: Shear stress is the shearing force per unit area.
e: True. Shear stress is the shearing force per unit area. Shear stress τ = F/A, force on a layer divided by the area of that layer.

q: Shear stress is the shearing force per unit volume.
e: False. Shear stress is shearing force per unit area, F/A, not per unit volume. The error is the part about Shear stress shearing force volume.

q: Viscosity is defined as the ratio of shearing stress to the velocity gradient.
e: True. Viscosity is defined as the ratio of shearing stress to the velocity gradient. Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, η = (F/A)/(dv/dy).

q: Stokes' law expresses the drag force resisting the fall of small spherical objects through a fluid medium under the influence of gravity.
e: True. Stokes' law expresses the drag force resisting the fall of small spherical objects through a fluid medium under the influence of gravity. Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a small sphere as F = 6πηrv.

q: Stokes' law expresses the drag force resisting the rise of small spherical objects through a fluid medium.
e: False. Stokes drag resists the fall of a small sphere through the fluid, not its rise. The error is the part about Stokes law expresses drag force resisting.

q: The drag force $F$ acting upward in resistance to the fall of a spherical object in a viscous liquid is $F = 6 \pi \eta r v$.
e: True. The drag force F acting upward in resistance to the fall of a spherical object in a viscous liquid is F = 6 π η r v. Stokes' law is F = 6πηrv, the upward viscous drag on a falling sphere.

q: At a constant velocity of fall (terminal velocity), the upward and downward forces are in balance.
e: True. At a constant velocity of fall (terminal velocity), the upward and downward forces are in balance. At terminal speed, weight, upthrust and Stokes drag add to zero.

q: Surface tension is the tendency of the surface of a liquid to behave like a stretched elastic skin (or membrane).
e: True. Surface tension is the tendency of the surface of a liquid to behave like a stretched elastic skin (or membrane). Surface tension γ is the force per unit length along a line in the surface, γ = F/l.

q: Cohesion refers to forces between molecules of the same substance.
e: True. Cohesion refers to forces between molecules of the same substance. Like-with-like attraction is cohesion.

q: Cohesion refers to forces between molecules of different substances.
e: False. Cohesion is attraction between like molecules; adhesion is between different substances. The error is the part about Cohesion refers forces molecules different substances.

q: Surface tension is the reason a water strider is able to stride along water surface without sinking.
e: True. Surface tension is the reason a water strider is able to stride along water surface without sinking. Surface tension γ is the force per unit length along a line in the surface, γ = F/l.

q: Paperclips, razor blades and light coins are able to rest on water although their density is higher than that of water.
e: True. Paperclips, razor blades and light coins are able to rest on water although their density is higher than that of water. Surface tension, not buoyancy, lets a dense needle rest on water.

q: Paperclips, razor blades and light coins are able to rest on water because their density is lower than that of water.
e: False. Pins and blades rest on water by surface tension even though they are denser than water. The error is the part about Paperclips razor blades light coins able.

q: Surface tension is defined as the force per unit length that acts across any line on a surface tending to pull the surface apart.
e: True. Surface tension is defined as the force per unit length that acts across any line on a surface tending to pull the surface apart. Surface tension γ is the force per unit length along a line in the surface, γ = F/l.

q: Surface tension is defined as the force per unit area that acts across any line on a surface.
e: False. Surface tension is force per unit length across a line, γ = F/l, not force per unit area. The error is the part about Surface tension defined force area acts.

q: The SI unit of surface tension is newton per metre ($N \cdot m^{-1}$).
e: True. The SI unit of surface tension is newton per metre (N · m⁻¹). Surface tension γ is the force per unit length along a line in the surface, γ = F/l.

q: The SI unit of surface tension is newton per metre squared ($N \cdot m^{-2}$).
e: False. The SI unit of surface tension is N m⁻¹, not N m⁻². The error is the part about surface tension newton metre squared m⁻².

q: Surface tension can also be referred to as a force because it is the tension between liquid molecules.
e: True. Surface tension can also be referred to as a force because it is the tension between liquid molecules. Surface tension γ is the force per unit length along a line in the surface, γ = F/l.

q: Capillary action is defined as the spontaneous flow of a liquid into a narrow tube or porous material.
e: True. Capillary action is defined as the spontaneous flow of a liquid into a narrow tube or porous material. Capillary rise is h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr); a narrower tube or larger γ gives a larger height.

q: Capillary action is caused by the combination of cohesive forces of the liquid and the adhesive forces between the liquid and tube material.
e: True. Capillary action is caused by the combination of cohesive forces of the liquid and the adhesive forces between the liquid and tube material. Capillary rise is h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr); a narrower tube or larger γ gives a larger height.

q: Cohesion and adhesion are two types of intramolecular forces.
e: False. Cohesion and adhesion are intermolecular forces, between molecules, not intramolecular bonds. The error is the part about Cohesion adhesion types intramolecular forces.

q: Adhesion refers to forces between molecules of different substances.
e: True. Adhesion refers to forces between molecules of different substances. Unlike-with-unlike attraction is adhesion, as in water on glass.

q: In order for wicking to occur, a tube needs to be sufficiently large in diameter.
e: False. Wicking needs a narrow tube; a large diameter kills capillary rise. The error is the part about order wicking occur tube needs sufficiently.

q: Capillarity is the rise or depression of a liquid in a narrow tube of small cross-sectional area.
e: True. Capillarity is the rise or depression of a liquid in a narrow tube of small cross-sectional area. Capillary rise is h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr); a narrower tube or larger γ gives a larger height.

q: Liquids that rise in small bore tubes inserted into the liquid are said to wet the tube.
e: True. Liquids that rise in small bore tubes inserted into the liquid are said to wet the tube. A liquid that climbs a capillary wets the wall; the meniscus is concave.

q: Liquids that are depressed within thin tubes below the surface of the surrounding liquid do wet the tube.
e: False. Liquids that are depressed in a capillary, such as mercury, do not wet the tube. The error is the part about Liquids depressed within thin tubes below.

q: Water is a liquid that wets glass capillary tubes.
e: True. Water is a liquid that wets glass capillary tubes. Capillary rise is h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr); a narrower tube or larger γ gives a larger height.

q: Mercury is a liquid that wets glass capillary tubes.
e: False. Mercury does not wet glass; its contact angle is obtuse and the meniscus is depressed. The error is the part about Mercury liquid wets glass capillary tubes.

q: Capillarity does not occur for non-wetting liquids.
e: True. Capillarity does not occur for non-wetting liquids. Capillary rise is h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr); a narrower tube or larger γ gives a larger height.

q: Capillarity occurs vigorously for non-wetting liquids.
e: False. Capillary rise is strong for wetting liquids; non-wetting liquids are depressed. The error is the part about Capillarity occurs vigorously non-wetting liquids.

q: When a glass tube is dipped into water, the adhesion between glass and water causes a thin film of water to be drawn up over the inner and outer surfaces of the tube.
e: True. When a glass tube is dipped into water, the adhesion between glass and water causes a thin film of water to be drawn up over the inner and outer surfaces of the tube. Water wets glass, so a film climbs the inner and outer walls.

q: Since the adhesive force is greater than cohesive force, water level rises until there is a sufficient mass of liquid for gravitational forces to overcome these intermolecular forces.
e: True. Since the adhesive force is greater than cohesive force, water level rises until there is a sufficient mass of liquid for gravitational forces to overcome these. Water-glass adhesion beats water-water cohesion, so the column climbs until weight balances it.

q: Since the cohesive force is greater than adhesive force, water level rises until there is a sufficient mass of liquid for gravitational forces to overcome these intermolecular forces.
e: False. Water rises because adhesion to glass beats cohesion in the water, not the other way round. The error is the part about Since cohesive force greater adhesive water.

q: The actual amount of rise depends on the surface tension $\gamma$, the contact angle $\theta$ and the radius $r$ of the tube.
e: True. The actual amount of rise depends on the surface tension γ, the contact angle θ and the radius r of the tube. Surface tension γ is the force per unit length along a line in the surface, γ = F/l.
